title: When Consistency Becomes Conformity
author: Mary Myatt
summary: Mary Myatt distinguishes 'consistency of entitlement' — every pupil having access to a rich curriculum, high expectations, and clear explanations — from surface consistency of lesson format, arguing schools routinely collapse the two together. Drawing on the organisational-theory concept of 'isomorphic mimicry,' borrowed from a conversation with Jon Hutchinson, she describes how trusts see a successful school using retrieval practice or knowledge organisers well and then mandate the visible form everywhere, without the understanding that made the original practice effective. Her key claim is that visible practices are not the source of success: retrieval practice works only when questions are carefully chosen and acted on, and once mandated as a universal routine, 'teachers comply with the form while the function gradually disappears.' She argues surface consistency is seductive to leaders precisely because it is easy to audit — whether a template is used, whether questions are on the board — while the things that actually matter, like whether explanations illuminate difficult ideas, are much harder to check, so proxies quietly replace substance. The piece offers a practical distinction between principles (what we value) and practices (one way of enacting it), and closes with a diagnostic leaders can apply before mandating any school-wide routine: if the visible routine disappeared, what other evidence would show the underlying principle was still secure?
points: Distinguishes 'consistency of entitlement' (curriculum quality, high expectations) from surface consistency of identical lesson format, arguing the two are wrongly treated as interchangeable.
Applies the organisational-theory concept of 'isomorphic mimicry' to explain how schools copy the visible form of successful practices without the understanding that made them work.
Argues surface consistency is attractive to leaders because it's easy to audit (templates, retrieval starters) while what actually matters is much harder to check.
Offers a working distinction between principles ('what we value') and practices ('one possible way of enacting it') to guide school-wide mandates.
Proposes a single diagnostic test: if a visible routine disappeared, what other evidence would show the underlying principle was still secure?
quotes: This is consistency of entitlement, and it matters enormously. But it is quite different from requiring every teacher to deliver that entitlement through the same lesson format, the same sequence of activities or the same routine at the same point in every lesson.

It is a concept from organisational theory that describes what happens when an organisation adopts the visible features associated with successful practice without necessarily developing the capability or understanding that made the original practice effective.

Teachers comply with the form while the function gradually disappears: retrieval questions are completed because it is the first five minutes, knowledge organisers are produced because they are expected, and lesson phases appear on slides because leaders look for them.
The things that are easiest to check can therefore become proxies for the things that matter most.

When practices are mistaken for principles, they become fixed. The question shifts from “Is this helping pupils learn what matters?” to “Is everyone doing it?” That is the point at which consistency starts to become conformity.
Perhaps the single most important diagnostic test is this: if the visible routine disappeared, what other evidence would tell us that the underlying principle was secure?
The aim is not identical practice. It is a shared commitment to strong principles, enacted intelligently.
